curriculum_source: CFA Program 2027 Level III, Volume 6 (PM Pathway), Learning Module 3: Active Equity Investing: Portfolio Construction

drills.los_text: describe elements of a manager's investment philosophy that influence the portfolio construction process

questions.stem: The active return of an actively managed portfolio is most likely driven by:

options.A: the benchmark's own returns, independent of portfolio weights.
options.B: the difference between portfolio weights and benchmark weights.
options.C: factors unrelated to portfolio and benchmark weights.

rationales.A: The benchmark return is the reference point against which active return is measured, not its source. Active return comes from active weights multiplied by security returns: R_A = Σ ΔW_i × R_i. A portfolio that holds exactly benchmark weights earns the benchmark return and an active return of zero, which shows that the benchmark's own returns cannot generate active return.
rationales.B: The excess return — also called active return (R_A) — of an actively managed portfolio is driven by the difference in weights between the active portfolio and the benchmark. It can be expressed mathematically as R_A = Σ ΔW_i × R_i, where R_i is the return on security i and ΔW_i is the difference between the portfolio weight W_Pi and the benchmark weight W_Bi. ΔW_i is also referred to as the active weight.
rationales.C: Active weights are precisely what generate active return: R_A = Σ ΔW_i × R_i. The relationship is direct rather than absent, and it is also exhaustive — if every ΔW_i equals zero, the portfolio tracks the benchmark and no active return is possible.

questions.stem: Positive active return is most likely generated when:

options.A: gains from correct active weights exceed losses from incorrect ones.
options.B: the portfolio is actively managed, whatever its active weights.
options.C: no particular condition holds, since none governs active return.

rationales.A: An active manager will generate positive active return if the gains generated by overweighting the securities that outperform the benchmark and underweighting the securities that underperform the benchmark are, on average, greater than the losses generated by underweighting the securities that outperform the benchmark and overweighting the securities that underperform the benchmark. Since R_A = Σ ΔW_i × R_i, the sign of active return depends on whether the active weights line up with realized relative performance.
rationales.B: Active management is zero-sum around the benchmark before costs, so the label "actively managed" guarantees nothing about the sign of active return. Positivity requires the condition on active weights to hold: the gains from overweighting outperformers and underweighting underperformers must exceed the losses from the opposite bets. Taking active positions is what creates the opportunity, not the result.
rationales.C: The governing principle is definite rather than absent. Active return is R_A = Σ ΔW_i × R_i, and it is positive when the gains from overweighting the securities that outperform and underweighting those that underperform exceed, on average, the losses from underweighting outperformers and overweighting underperformers.

questions.stem: A source of active return in an actively managed equity portfolio is most likely:

options.A: matching benchmark weights to eliminate active risk.
options.B: tilting active weights toward rewarded risks the benchmark lacks.
options.C: minimizing turnover to reduce transaction costs.

rationales.A: Matching benchmark weights sets every active weight to zero. With ΔW_i = 0 for all i, the portfolio earns the benchmark return and no active return at all, so this cannot be a source of active return. The market premium accrues to the benchmark itself and is available without any active decision.
rationales.B: Conceptually, a manager can generate active return in three ways: strategically adjusting the active weights of securities to create long-term exposures to rewarded risks that differ from those of the benchmark; tactically adjusting active weights, using skill in identifying mispricing in securities, sectors or rewarded risks, to generate alpha that cannot be explained by long-term exposure to rewarded risks; and assuming excessive idiosyncratic risk, which may result in lucky or unlucky returns. The decomposition is R_A = Σ(β_pk − β_bk) × F_k + (α + ε), where the first term is the return from differences in rewarded factor exposures and the bracketed term collects alpha and idiosyncratic return.
rationales.C: Cost control is an implementation consideration, not one of the three sources of active return, which are differential exposure to rewarded factors, alpha from identifying mispricing, and idiosyncratic risk. Lower turnover can preserve active return that has already been generated, but it does not appear in R_A = Σ(β_pk − β_bk) × F_k + (α + ε) as a source of it.

questions.stem: Rewarded factors are most likely best described as:

options.A: risks carrying a long-run return premium.
options.B: any risk a portfolio carries, compensated or not.
options.C: risks that systematically reduce long-run returns.

rationales.A: Rewarded factors is a generic term referring specifically to investment risks for which investors expect to be compensated through a long-run return premium, such as exposure to market risk and liquidity risk. The existence of numerous rewarded factors is well documented in the literature and supported by strong empirical evidence. Recognition of this phenomenon is fundamentally altering the investment management industry, with large asset owners negotiating fee structures that compensate active managers for returns above and beyond those that can be generated by simple exposure to rewarded factors.
rationales.B: The defining property is expected compensation in the form of a long-run return premium. Risks a portfolio happens to carry without such a premium are uncompensated, or unrewarded, risks — the contrast class to rewarded factors. Bearing uncompensated risk raises active risk without raising expected active return, which is why the distinction matters for position sizing.
rationales.C: Rewarded means premium-earning. Market risk and liquidity risk are the reading's examples: investors expect to be paid for bearing them over the long run, so exposure to them raises rather than reduces expected long-run returns.

questions.stem: The four building blocks of portfolio construction most likely are:

options.A: Security selection, market timing, currency management, and tax optimization.
options.B: Asset allocation, security selection, benchmark selection, and performance attribution.
options.C: Rewarded factor weightings, alpha skills, position sizing, and breadth of expertise.

rationales.A: These are generic active-management activities rather than the four building blocks of portfolio construction. Market timing, currency management and tax optimization are implementation or mandate questions; none of them maps onto the terms of R_A = Σ(β_pk − β_bk) × F_k + (α + ε).
rationales.B: This conflates the broad steps of the investment process with the four specific building blocks. Asset allocation and benchmark selection precede portfolio construction, and performance attribution follows it; the building blocks are the levers a manager pulls inside a mandate.
rationales.C: The three main building blocks of portfolio construction are rewarded factor weightings, alpha skills, and position sizing, and together they encompass all of R_A = Σ(β_pk − β_bk) × F_k + (α + ε): rewarded factor weightings correspond to the differential factor exposures, alpha skills to α, and position sizing to the idiosyncratic term. A fourth critical component, breadth of expertise, is necessary to assemble these three building blocks into a successful portfolio construction process.

questions.stem: Expected active return under the full fundamental law of active management is most likely determined by:

options.A: a qualitative principle to spread bets widely, with no formal expression.
options.B: the information coefficient, breadth, active risk, and the transfer coefficient.
options.C: the information coefficient alone.

rationales.A: The law has an explicit mathematical expression, E(R_A) = IC × √BR × σ_RA × TC, not merely a qualitative instruction. Breadth does matter, but in a quantified way: expected active return rises with the square root of the number of truly independent decisions, so adding correlated bets adds far less than adding uncorrelated ones.
rationales.B: E(R_A) = IC × √BR × σ_RA × TC, where IC is the expected information coefficient of the manager — the extent to which a manager's forecasted active returns correspond to the manager's realized active returns; BR is breadth — the number of truly independent decisions made each year; TC is the transfer coefficient, or the ability to translate portfolio insights into investment decisions without constraint (a truly unconstrained portfolio would have a transfer coefficient of 1); and σ_RA is the manager's active risk. The basic fundamental law was introduced by Grinold (1989) and was expanded into the full fundamental law with the addition of the transfer coefficient by Clarke, de Silva and Thorley (2002).
rationales.C: The information coefficient is one of four inputs. Breadth, active risk and the transfer coefficient complete the expression E(R_A) = IC × √BR × σ_RA × TC, so a skilled forecaster with few independent decisions, low active risk, or binding constraints that hold the transfer coefficient well below 1 will still deliver little active return.

questions.stem: A manager has an information coefficient of 0.10, a transfer coefficient of 0.25, and active risk of 6%. Expected active return from a single truly independent decision each year is closest to:

options.A: 0 bps.
options.B: 60 bps.
options.C: 15 bps.

rationales.A: A single independent decision has an explicit and non-zero expected value: E(R_A) = IC × √BR × σ_RA × TC = 0.10 × √1 × 6% × 0.25 = 0.15%, or 15 bps. An expectation of zero would require no skill (IC = 0), no breadth, no active risk, or a transfer coefficient of zero — none of which holds here.
rationales.B: Multiplying only skill by active risk, 0.10 × 6% = 0.60%, omits the transfer coefficient. With TC = 0.25, representative of a constrained long-only investor, just a quarter of the insight reaches the portfolio, so the expectation is 0.10 × √1 × 6% × 0.25 = 15 bps rather than 60 bps.
rationales.C: E(R_A) = IC × √BR × σ_RA × TC = 0.10 × √1 × 6% × 0.25 = 0.15%, so the manager could expect to generate active return of 15 bps yearly, on average, from a single independent decision. Active risk of 6% is high by institutional standards and a transfer coefficient of 0.25 is representative of a constrained long-only investor. Because breadth enters as a square root, reaching 1% of excess return would require approximately 40 fully independent decisions: 0.10 × √40 × 6% × 0.25 ≈ 0.95%.

questions.stem: Independent decisions, as used in the fundamental law of active management, most likely refer to:

options.A: the number of securities held.
options.B: the number of sectors holding active positions.
options.C: the number of uncorrelated active decisions.

rationales.A: This is the misconception the fundamental law rejects. Independent decisions are not the same thing as individual securities, so the nominal count of holdings overstates breadth whenever those holdings share common drivers. In evaluating portfolio construction, one must distinguish between the nominal number of decisions a manager makes about active weights and the effective number of independent decisions.
rationales.B: Independence is defined by the correlation between decisions, not by the label on a bucket. Sector counts can overstate breadth, because positions in different sectors can be driven by the same macro factor, and can understate it, because two bets within one sector may be genuinely uncorrelated.
rationales.C: Independent decisions are uncorrelated decisions, much like two uncorrelated stocks are diversifying, and are not the same thing as individual securities. Overweighting both General Motors and Toyota, two auto companies, relative to their benchmark weights is not a pair of fully independent decisions, because much of their respective returns is driven by common influences — the strength of consumer spending, the price of gasoline, and the prices of steel and aluminum, for example. Confidence in a manager's ability to outperform increases when performance can be attributed to a larger sample of independent decisions, so one must distinguish the nominal number of active-weight decisions from the effective number of independent ones. Breadth enters E(R_A) = IC × √BR × σ_RA × TC as BR.

questions.stem: The role of diversification in position sizing is most likely best described as:

options.A: powerful but limited by the volatility of the underlying stocks.
options.B: powerful without limit, driving portfolio volatility toward zero.
options.C: immaterial, imposing no limit on position sizing.

rationales.A: Diversification is a powerful tool, but it has its limitations. Even the most diversified portfolio of high-volatility stocks — a 500-stock portfolio with average single-stock volatility of 30% — cannot achieve the same level of volatility inherent in portfolios of lower-volatility stocks. Even the most concentrated portfolio of lower-volatility stocks displays a portfolio volatility lower than that of the highly diversified portfolio of higher-volatility stocks. The concentrated portfolio, however, bears higher idiosyncratic risk, which can substantially influence portfolio performance.
rationales.B: Adding names diversifies away idiosyncratic risk but leaves the common-factor component untouched, so volatility converges on a positive floor set by the stocks held rather than on zero. A broadly diversified portfolio of stocks with 30% average single-stock volatility remains more volatile than a concentrated portfolio of low-volatility stocks.
rationales.C: The limit is the point of the comparison. Spreading positions reduces idiosyncratic risk, but the volatility of the underlying stocks caps what any amount of diversification can achieve, and the concentration a manager chooses therefore trades lower idiosyncratic risk against the breadth needed to express insight.

questions.stem: A four-factor regression of monthly returns over 26 years gives market, size, value and momentum betas of 0.99, −0.16, 0.02 and −0.01 for a broad large-cap index; 0.92, −0.23, 0.41 and 0.13 for a large-cap value index; and 0.90, 0.13, 0.59 and 0.09 for an actively managed value fund, with monthly alphas of 0.05%, −0.05% and −0.35%, respectively. These results most likely indicate:

options.A: positive selection alpha and negligible value exposure for the value fund.
options.B: a large-cap tilt and negligible value exposure for the broad index.
options.C: a small-cap tilt and negligible value exposure for the value index.

rationales.A: The value fund carries a large value beta of 0.59, the biggest value exposure of the three, and its monthly alpha is −0.35%, not +0.35%. Its return is explained by factor exposures rather than by positive selection skill: with monthly factor performance of 0.64% for market, 0.16% for size, 0.18% for value and 0.61% for momentum, the fund's loadings account for its results and the residual is negative. Its R² of 0.74 is also the lowest of the three, so more of its variation is left unexplained by the four factors.
rationales.B: The Russell 1000 Index has a market beta of 0.99, a size beta of −0.16 — a large-cap tilt, since the size factor pays for small-cap exposure — a value beta of 0.02, a momentum beta of −0.01, a monthly alpha of 0.05% and an R² of 0.99. A value loading of essentially zero is what a broad market-capitalization-weighted index should show, and the near-unit market beta with 0.99 R² confirms that the index is almost entirely market exposure.
rationales.C: The Russell 1000 Value Index has a size beta of −0.23, which is a large-cap tilt rather than a small-cap tilt, and a substantial value beta of 0.41 rather than a negligible one. Its market beta is 0.92, momentum beta 0.13, monthly alpha −0.05% and R² 0.95, so it is clearly distinguished from the broad Russell 1000, whose value beta is 0.02.

drills.los_text: discuss approaches for constructing actively managed equity portfolios

questions.stem: Systematic strategies are most likely:

options.A: built on rules targeting balanced exposure to known rewarded factors.
options.B: built on discretionary judgment applied security by security.
options.C: built without rules of any kind.

rationales.A: Systematic strategies are designed around the construction of portfolios that seek to extract return premiums from a balanced exposure to known, rewarded factors. They typically incorporate research-based rules applied across a broad universe of securities, which gives them breadth rather than depth. Because the rules are applied consistently to many names, these strategies seek to reduce exposure to idiosyncratic risk and often use broadly diversified portfolios to achieve the desired factor exposure while minimizing security-specific risk. Their explicit, rules-based specification also makes them more adaptable to a formal portfolio optimization process, and they are unlikely to run concentrated portfolios.
rationales.B: Discretionary judgment applied security by security is the contrasting approach, not the systematic one. Discretionary strategies integrate the judgment of the manager, usually on a smaller subset of securities, and build portfolios through a less formal process that is often more concentrated. A systematic strategy runs on research-based rules applied across a broad universe, so judgment enters when the rules are designed rather than at each position.
rationales.C: Rules are the essence of a systematic strategy: balanced, repeatable exposure to known rewarded factors is obtained precisely by applying research-based rules across a broad universe of securities. Remove the rules and nothing remains that is systematic, and nothing remains that can be fed into a formal portfolio optimization process.

questions.stem: Discretionary strategies are most likely to:

options.A: follow a process identical to that of systematic strategies.
options.B: build depth of insight into a firm's governance, business model, and competitive landscape.
options.C: apply fixed rules without manager judgment.

rationales.A: Depth through judgment versus breadth through rules is the core contrast between the two approaches, so their processes and philosophies are not identical. Discretionary managers integrate the manager's judgment on a smaller subset of securities and construct portfolios less formally, while systematic managers encode research-based rules and apply them across a broad universe.
rationales.B: Discretionary strategies search for active returns by building a greater depth of understanding of a firm's governance, business model, and competitive landscape, by developing better factor proxies (for example, a better definition of Quality), or through successful timing strategies. Factor timing is a challenging endeavor, and few factor-based systematic strategies have integrated a factor timing approach. Discretionary strategies integrate the judgment of the manager, usually on a smaller subset of securities, and are generally more concentrated, reflecting the depth of the manager's insights into company characteristics and the competitive landscape. Discretionary managers typically use a less formal approach to portfolio construction, building a portfolio of securities deemed attractive subject to a set of agreed-upon risk constraints.
rationales.C: Depth of judgment about governance, business models, and the competitive landscape is the discretionary hallmark; applying fixed rules without judgment describes the systematic approach instead. A discretionary portfolio reflects insights developed on a smaller subset of securities, assembled through a less formal construction process, rather than a rule applied uniformly across a universe.

questions.stem: The difference between top-down and bottom-up equity approaches is most likely that:

options.A: neither is an actual investment strategy.
options.B: the two are indistinguishable in practice.
options.C: top-down starts from the macro environment.

rationales.A: Both top-down and bottom-up are standard, well-defined strategy architectures used in practice, and both typically rely on returns from factors. The labels describe where the analysis begins, not whether a strategy exists.
rationales.B: The starting point differs fundamentally. A top-down manager projects the expected macro environment downward onto countries, asset classes, sectors, and then securities, whereas a bottom-up manager aggregates upward from the risk and return characteristics of individual securities. Top-down managers are more likely to emphasize macro factors, while bottom-up managers emphasize security-specific factors.
rationales.C: A top-down approach seeks to understand the overall geo-political, economic, financial, social, and public policy environment and then projects how that expected environment will affect countries, asset classes, sectors, and then securities. A manager who projects that growth companies will outperform value companies, that financials will outperform industrials, that the US market will outperform the European market, that oil prices will increase, or that cash will outperform equity, and who then targets individual securities or a cash/stock allocation to reflect these views, is following a top-down approach. A manager following a bottom-up approach instead develops an understanding of the environment by first evaluating the risk and return characteristics of individual securities. Both top-down and bottom-up strategies typically rely on returns from factors, but top-down managers are more likely to emphasize macro factors, whereas bottom-up managers emphasize security-specific factors.

questions.stem: A pairing of equity management approach with its typical use of macro factors, factor timing, and portfolio concentration is most likely:

options.A: discretionary bottom-up, macro-driven, no factor timing, always concentrated.
options.B: systematic bottom-up, macro-driven, factor timing, concentrated.
options.C: discretionary top-down, macro-driven, factor timing, diversified.

rationales.A: Discretionary bottom-up managers emphasize firm-specific characteristics and factors rather than macro forecasts, may well implement factor timing, and can be either diversified or concentrated depending on their strategy and portfolio management style. Nothing in the quadrant forces concentration, and nothing excludes factor timing.
rationales.B: Systematic bottom-up managers emphasize security-specific factors rather than macro factors, apply no factor timing, and hold diversified portfolios. Systematic managers in general are unlikely to run concentrated portfolios, so concentration is the wrong characteristic for this quadrant as well.
rationales.C: Discretionary top-down managers emphasize macro factors, are the managers most likely to implement factor timing, and hold diversified portfolios. Discretionary bottom-up managers emphasize firm-specific characteristics and factors, may use factor timing, and are diversified or concentrated depending on strategy and style. Systematic top-down managers would in principle emphasize macro factors and factor timing and hold diversified portfolios, although there are few managers in that category. Systematic bottom-up managers emphasize security-specific factors, apply no factor timing, and are diversified. The organizing logic is that exposure to rewarded factors can be achieved either systematically or discretionarily; bottom-up managers first emphasize security-specific factors while top-down managers first emphasize macro factors; factor timing is more likely among discretionary managers, especially those with a top-down approach; and systematic managers are unlikely to run concentrated portfolios, whereas discretionary managers can be concentrated or diversified.

questions.stem: Equity portfolio construction, as commonly practiced, is most likely to:

options.A: maximize a risk-adjusted return.
options.B: proceed without any objective function.
options.C: follow no specified objective framework.

rationales.A: A common objective function in portfolio management is to maximize a risk-adjusted return. If risk is being measured by predicted active risk, then the objective function seeks to maximize the information ratio, the ratio of active return to active risk. If risk is being measured by predicted portfolio volatility, then the objective function seeks to maximize the Sharpe ratio, the ratio of return in excess of the risk-free rate to portfolio volatility. Ideally, these objective functions would specify net returns, adjusted for the costs associated with implementation.
rationales.B: Construction does run against an objective function: maximizing a risk-adjusted return is the common one. It is expressed as the information ratio, active return over active risk, when risk is measured as predicted active risk, and as the Sharpe ratio, excess return over portfolio volatility, when risk is measured as predicted portfolio volatility.
rationales.C: The framework is explicit rather than absent. With predicted active risk as the risk measure, the objective is to maximize the information ratio, the ratio of active return to active risk; with predicted portfolio volatility as the risk measure, it is to maximize the Sharpe ratio, ideally stated on returns net of implementation costs.

questions.stem: Typical constraints in portfolio optimization most likely include:

options.A: limits on realized active returns and alpha.
options.B: only the diversification minimums required by law.
options.C: limits on geographic, sector, industry, and single-security exposures.

rationales.A: Constraints are placed on exposures and on implementation, for example limits on transaction costs in order to limit turnover and help manage liquidity issues. They are not placed on realized active returns or alpha, which are outcomes of the process rather than inputs to it and so cannot be constrained directly in the optimization.
rationales.B: The constraints in the portfolio optimization problem are manager- and mandate-imposed, not merely legal diversification minimums: limits on geographic, sector, industry, and single-security exposures, limits on transaction costs, and limits on exposure to specific factors. Such constraints deliberately narrow the optimizer's feasible set, which is the point of them, since they keep the portfolio consistent with the stated investment process or with the client's requirements.
rationales.C: Typical constraints in the portfolio optimization problem may include limits on geographic, sector, industry, and single-security exposures, and may also specify limits on transaction costs, to limit turnover and help manage liquidity issues. They may also include limits on exposure to specific factors: for example, the investment process may specify a required minimum market capitalization for any single security, or a minimum weighted average capitalization for the portfolio as a whole; or it may specify a maximum price-to-book ratio for any single security, or a maximum weighted average price-to-book ratio for the portfolio. Constraints can be defined relative to the benchmark or without regard to it.

questions.stem: Risk-based objective functions such as minimum variance and maximum diversification are most likely to:

options.A: forecast an explicit expected return for each rewarded factor.
options.B: favor growth and high-beta securities.
options.C: create factor exposures implicitly, with no explicit return forecast.

rationales.A: Risk-based objective functions such as minimum variance and maximum diversification contain no explicit expected return component. They state their objectives purely in terms of risk metrics, such as portfolio volatility, downside risk, maximum diversification, and drawdowns. Any factor exposure they produce arises implicitly from the risk-minimizing process rather than from a return forecast for any factor.
rationales.B: Because these objective functions seek to manage or minimize risk, they tend to favor value and low-beta securities, not growth and high-beta ones. Products built using them often exhibit a Market beta below 1.0, together with statistically significant exposure to the Value factor and to the low-minus-high-beta (BAB) factor.
rationales.C: These optimization approaches specify their objectives in terms of risk metrics, such as portfolio volatility, downside risk, maximum diversification, and drawdowns, and so do not integrate an explicit expected return component. They do, however, implicitly create an exposure to risk factors: products built using a risk-based objective function such as minimum variance or maximum diversification often exhibit a Market beta below 1.0 and have statistically significant exposure to the Value factor and to the low-minus-high-beta (BAB) factor. This occurs because an objective function that seeks to manage or minimize risk will tend to favor value and low-beta securities.

questions.stem: With respect to the specification of objectives and constraints, systematic and discretionary managers are most likely:

options.A: equally explicit.
options.B: indistinguishable.
options.C: explicit and less explicit, respectively.

rationales.A: The two are not equally explicit. A systematic manager's objectives and constraints are explicitly specified, because they have to be written down to be coded into the investment process and passed to an optimizer, whereas a discretionary manager's are specified far less formally.
rationales.B: A real difference separates the two: the objectives and constraints of systematic managers are explicitly specified, while those of discretionary managers are less explicitly specified. The difference is substantive rather than presentational, since the systematic process cannot run at all without the objective and the constraints being stated.
rationales.C: Not all portfolio managers engage in a formalistic, scientific approach to portfolio construction. The objectives and constraints of systematic managers are explicitly specified, whereas those of discretionary managers are less explicitly specified. However, most managers at least conceptually optimize their portfolios using the expected returns for each security, their own view of risk, and the constraints imposed by the stated portfolio construction process or by the client.

questions.stem: The philosophical divide between systematic and discretionary equity managers is most likely:

options.A: shrinking.
options.B: unchanged.
options.C: widening.

rationales.A: The philosophical divide between systematic and discretionary managers seems to be shrinking. The two were commonly differentiated in terms of their breadth and depth, with discretionary managers conducting more in-depth research on a subset of the securities universe and systematic managers having more breadth, that is, less in-depth research across the entire universe of securities. Although this remains generally true today, research and technology have been narrowing the gap. Advancements in and the accessibility of technology, together with the greater range of quality data available, are allowing discretionary managers to extend their in-depth analyses across a broader universe of securities. Technology also allows systematic managers to design strategies that can capture risk premiums in rewarded factors, a source of active returns that was previously considered to be part of the alpha of discretionary managers.
rationales.B: The breadth and depth distinction remains generally true, but the gap has not stayed static: research and technology have been narrowing it, so the divide is shrinking rather than unchanged. Those same breadth and depth differences are precisely what technology has been eroding on both sides, so they are no bar to convergence.
rationales.C: The divide is shrinking, not widening, and neither side is narrowing its toolkit. Technology and the greater range of quality data available let discretionary managers extend in-depth analysis across a broader universe of securities, and let systematic managers design strategies that capture risk premiums in rewarded factors, a source of return once considered part of discretionary alpha.

questions.stem: Both systematic and discretionary equity managers are most likely to:

options.A: operate under entirely unrelated frameworks.
options.B: operate under no framework at all.
options.C: operate under active risk and Active Share limits relative to a benchmark.

rationales.A: The frameworks are not unrelated. Each manager's investment approach, systematic or discretionary, is implemented within a framework that specifies the acceptable levels of active risk and Active Share relative to a clearly articulated benchmark, so this discipline is common to both.
rationales.B: A shared active risk and Active Share framework disciplines both approaches: each manager's investment approach is implemented within specified acceptable levels of active risk and Active Share relative to a clearly articulated benchmark, and a manager may emphasize those dimensions to varying degrees.
rationales.C: Each manager's investment approach is implemented within a framework that specifies the acceptable levels of active risk and Active Share relative to a clearly articulated benchmark, where Active Share is a measure of how similar a portfolio is to its benchmark. A manager may emphasize these dimensions to varying degrees as he attempts to differentiate his portfolio from the benchmark. In addition, these approaches can vary in the extent to which they are benchmark aware versus benchmark agnostic.

drills.los_text: distinguish between Active Share and active risk and discuss how each measure relates to a manager's investment strategy

questions.stem: Active Share is most likely:

options.A: an undefined portfolio measure.
options.B: one-half the sum of the absolute differences between portfolio and benchmark security weights.
options.C: a defined measure for which no formula exists.

rationales.A: Active Share is a standard, well-defined measure of active management. It is calculated as ½ × Σ |Weight_portfolio,i − Weight_benchmark,i|, summed over the total number of securities that are in either the portfolio or the benchmark. It measures the differentiation of a portfolio's holdings from the holdings of its chosen benchmark, that is, the proportion of the portfolio's holdings that is different from the benchmark. It equals 0 for a portfolio that matches the benchmark and 100% for a portfolio that shares no investments with the benchmark.
rationales.B: Active Share = ½ × Σ |Weight_portfolio,i − Weight_benchmark,i|, where n represents the total number of securities that are in either the portfolio or the benchmark. The calculation involves no statistical analysis or estimation; it is simple arithmetic on the two sets of weights. Active Share is a measure of the differentiation of the holdings of a portfolio from the holdings of a chosen benchmark portfolio: it measures the proportion of a portfolio's holdings that is different from the benchmark for that portfolio. Active Share is 0 for a portfolio that matches the benchmark and 100% for a portfolio that shares no investments with those of the benchmark.
rationales.C: A formula does exist, and it requires no statistical estimation: Active Share = ½ × Σ |Weight_portfolio,i − Weight_benchmark,i|, summed across all securities held in either the portfolio or the benchmark. Only the two sets of security weights are needed, which is why Active Share is simple arithmetic rather than a modeled or estimated quantity.

questions.stem: The two sources of Active Share most likely are:

options.A: sector allocation differences and factor exposure differences versus the benchmark.
options.B: the portfolio's active risk and the correlation of its active returns with the benchmark.
options.C: off-benchmark holdings and benchmark securities held at non-benchmark weights.

rationales.A: Sector and factor deviations describe sources of active risk, not sources of Active Share. Active Share depends only on holdings weights, and it has only two sources: including securities in the portfolio that are not in the benchmark, and holding benchmark securities at weights different from their benchmark weights. Any sector or factor deviation is itself produced by those two weight decisions, so describing the sources as sector and factor differences is one step removed from the measure being calculated.
rationales.B: Active Share is a holdings-based measure, computed from the differences between portfolio and benchmark security weights; it is not derived from active risk or from return correlations. Correlations and variances are inputs to predicted active risk, which is a forward-looking estimate and is not fully within the manager's control. A portfolio manager does have complete control over Active Share, because she determines the weights of the securities in her portfolio.
rationales.C: There are only two sources of Active Share: including securities in the portfolio that are not in the benchmark, and holding securities in the portfolio that are in the benchmark but at weights different than the benchmark weights. If two portfolios are managed against the same benchmark and invest only in securities that are part of the benchmark, the portfolio with fewer securities will have a higher level of Active Share than the highly diversified portfolio. A portfolio manager has complete control over his Active Share because he determines the weights of the securities in his portfolio.

questions.stem: Active Share and active risk are most likely:

options.A: equally within the portfolio manager's control.
options.B: fully within the manager's control only in the case of Active Share.
options.C: the same measure expressed in different units.

rationales.A: The degree of control is not the same. Active Share is fully controllable, because the manager chooses the portfolio weights that determine it. Active risk is not: the relevant forward-looking measure, predicted active risk, depends on the correlations and variances of the securities held, and the manager does not set those.
rationales.B: A portfolio manager can completely control Active Share but cannot completely control active risk, because active risk depends on the correlations and variances of securities that are beyond her control. Active risk is the more complicated calculation and comes in two forms. Realized active risk is the actual, historical standard deviation between the portfolio return and the benchmark return, and it is easy to calculate. But portfolio construction is a forward-looking exercise, and in that context the relevant measure is predicted active risk, which requires forward-looking estimates of correlations and variances. Like Active Share, active risk depends on the differences between the security weights in the portfolio and those in the benchmark, but only active risk also depends on the covariance structure of the securities.
rationales.C: The two are related but distinct. Active Share is a holdings-difference measure, one-half the sum of the absolute differences between portfolio and benchmark security weights. Active risk is a return-volatility measure, the standard deviation of the difference between the portfolio return and the benchmark return. Two portfolios with identical Active Share can show very different active risk, because active risk also depends on the correlations and variances of the securities held.

questions.stem: Underweighting one bank stock to overweight another bank stock, rather than to overweight an information technology stock by the same amount, most likely has:

options.A: an identical effect on both Active Share and active risk.
options.B: an identical effect on active risk.
options.C: a smaller effect on active risk.

rationales.A: Half of this is right and half is wrong. Active Share is not concerned with cross correlation, so if the extent of the underweighting and overweighting is the same in both cases, the effect on Active Share is indeed identical. Active risk, however, is affected by the degree of cross correlation, so the two substitutions do not affect it equally: the correlation of the bank/technology pair is most likely lower than that of the bank/bank pair.
rationales.B: The within-sector swap moves active risk less, because the two bank stocks are highly correlated with each other, whereas the bank/technology substitution also shifts factor exposures and pairs two less correlated securities. Active risk is affected by the degree of cross correlation; Active Share is not. Only the effect on Active Share is identical across the two substitutions.
rationales.C: Underweighting one bank stock to overweight another bank stock will likely have less effect on active risk than underweighting one bank stock and overweighting an information technology stock. Active risk is affected by the degree of cross correlation, but Active Share is not: Active Share is not concerned with the efficiency of diversification. If the extent of the underweighting and overweighting is the same in the bank/bank case and in the bank/technology case, the effect on Active Share would be identical. The effect on active risk would be different, however, because the correlation of the bank/technology pair is most likely lower than the correlation of the bank/bank pair. This highlights an important difference between Active Share and active risk.

questions.stem: For an unconstrained investor under a single-factor model, active risk most likely:

options.A: is independent of factor exposure and depends only on the number of securities held.
options.B: reaches its maximum level when factor exposure is fully neutralized.
options.C: is high when net factor exposure is high, whatever the level of idiosyncratic risk.

rationales.A: Active risk is not independent of factor exposure: high net exposure to a risk factor leads to a high level of active risk, irrespective of the level of idiosyncratic risk. The number of securities held matters only for the portion of active risk attributed to Active Share, and that attribution applies once factor exposure has been neutralized; that portion is smaller if the number of securities is large and/or average idiosyncratic risk is small.
rationales.B: Full neutralization does not maximize active risk. If the factor exposure is fully neutralized, the active risk is attributed entirely to Active Share, and the active risk attributed to Active Share is smaller if the number of securities is large and/or average idiosyncratic risk is small. Neutralizing the factor exposure therefore removes the component that drives active risk highest, namely high net factor exposure.
rationales.C: High net exposure to a risk factor leads to a high level of active risk, irrespective of the level of idiosyncratic risk. The derived relationship among active risk, Active Share, and factor exposure for an unconstrained investor, assuming a single-factor model, also holds that: if the factor exposure is fully neutralized, the active risk will be entirely attributed to Active Share; the active risk attributed to Active Share will be smaller if the number of securities is large and/or average idiosyncratic risk is small; and the level of active risk will rise with an increase in factor and idiosyncratic volatility, such as occurred in 2008.

questions.stem: Equity investment styles are most likely classified by:

options.A: their joint levels of Active Share and active risk.
options.B: neither measure jointly, as Active Share and active risk are independent.
options.C: neither measure, as active managers do not differ systematically on them.

rationales.A: Styles map onto a two-dimensional space whose axes are Active Share and active risk. Low Active Share with low active risk is pure indexing or closet indexing, a closet indexer being a fund that advertises itself as being actively managed but is substantially similar to an index fund in its exposures. High Active Share with low active risk is factor-neutral, diversified stock picking. Low-to-medium Active Share with medium active risk is diversified factor bets. High Active Share with high active risk is either concentrated factor bets or concentrated stock picking.
rationales.B: The two measures are not independent: both depend on the differences between the security weights in the portfolio and those in the benchmark, and active risk additionally depends on the correlations and variances of the securities. Because they share that common input but diverge on the covariance structure, the pair can be plotted jointly, and positions in that plane identify styles ranging from pure and closet indexing, through diversified factor bets, to concentrated stock picking.
rationales.C: Active managers are differentiated by these two measures rather than treated as a single undifferentiated group. A fund with low Active Share and low active risk is an index fund or a closet indexer; one with high Active Share and low active risk is a diversified, factor-neutral stock picker; one with low-to-medium Active Share and medium active risk is a diversified factor better; and one with high Active Share and high active risk is a concentrated stock picker or a concentrated factor better.

questions.stem: The holdings of a typical multi-factor product are most likely:

options.A: varied, with no characteristic degree of concentration.
options.B: concentrated in a few high-conviction securities.
options.C: diversified across a large number of securities.

rationales.A: The pattern is characteristic rather than varied. Most multi-factor products have a low concentration among securities, often holding more than 250 positions, because the purpose of these products is to achieve a balanced exposure to risk factors and minimize idiosyncratic risks. That shows up as a high Active Share, such as 0.70, combined with reasonably low active risk, often in the range of ±3%.
rationales.B: Multi-factor products are the low-concentration case, often holding more than 250 positions and diversified across both factors and securities. Concentration in a few high-conviction names describes the concentrated stock picker instead, which typically shows Active Share above 0.90 and active risk of 8%-12% or higher.
rationales.C: Most multi-factor products have a low concentration among securities, often holding more than 250 positions; the purpose of these products is to achieve a balanced exposure to risk factors and minimize idiosyncratic risks. They are diversified across factors and securities. They therefore typically have a high Active Share, such as 0.70, but reasonably low active risk (tracking error), often in the range of ±3%.

questions.stem: A concentrated stock picker most likely has:

options.A: high Active Share and high active risk.
options.B: high Active Share and low active risk.
options.C: low Active Share and high active risk.

rationales.A: The concentrated stock picker has both a high Active Share, typically above 0.90, and a high active risk, such as 8%-12% or higher. The average active manager owns about 100 stocks, and fewer than 20% of managers own more than 200 stocks. It follows that the level of idiosyncratic risk in the average active discretionary portfolio is greater than that of the average multi-factor fund with its 250-plus positions, so on average the portfolio of a typical discretionary manager displays higher active risk.
rationales.B: A high Active Share of around 0.70 paired with low active risk of about ±3% describes a diversified multi-factor product, or a factor-neutral diversified stock picker: many positions, balanced factor exposures, little idiosyncratic risk. The concentrated stock picker instead runs both a high Active Share, typically above 0.90, and a high active risk of 8%-12% or more.
rationales.C: Concentration in relatively few names pushes portfolio weights far from benchmark weights, so Active Share is high, not low, typically above 0.90. It sits alongside high active risk of 8%-12% or more, which follows from the elevated idiosyncratic risk of holding about 100 stocks rather than the 250-plus positions of a diversified multi-factor fund.

questions.stem: The fund most likely paired correctly with its reported active risk and Active Share is:

options.A: AIM Constellation, 5.4% active risk and 0.93 Active Share.
options.B: Vanguard Index Fund, 0.0% active risk and 0.00 Active Share.
options.C: T. Rowe Price Mid-Cap Value, 9.7% active risk and 0.66 Active Share.

rationales.A: AIM Constellation is a large-cap growth fund that took significant sector bets, and its reported figures are 9.7% active risk with a moderate 0.66 Active Share. The 5.4% active risk and 0.93 Active Share pairing belongs to T. Rowe Price Mid-Cap Value, a mid-cap value fund that placed limited active weights on sectors but did significant stock picking.
rationales.B: The Vanguard Index Fund is indexed, so it reports 0.0% active risk and 0.00 Active Share. The other reported examples: RiverSource Disciplined Equity, large-cap growth with a small active weight and limited factor timing, 4.4% active risk and 0.54 Active Share; T. Rowe Price Mid-Cap Value, mid-cap value with limited active weights on sectors but significant stock picking, 5.4% active risk and 0.93 Active Share; AIM Constellation, large-cap growth with significant sector bets, 9.7% active risk and 0.66 Active Share; and GMO Quality, mega-cap core with timing on a number of factors and cash, 12.9% active risk.
rationales.C: Those figures belong to AIM Constellation, the large-cap growth fund that took significant sector bets. T. Rowe Price Mid-Cap Value combined limited active weights on sectors with significant stock picking, and its reported figures are 5.4% active risk and 0.93 Active Share.

drills.los_text: discuss the application of risk budgeting concepts in portfolio construction

questions.stem: Risk budgeting is most likely the process of:

options.A: eliminating active risk so that the portfolio tracks its benchmark exactly.
options.B: allocating the portfolio's total risk appetite among the components of portfolio choice.
options.C: maximizing total portfolio return without regard to any risk limit.

rationales.A: Risk budgeting allocates a risk budget efficiently; it does not eliminate active risk. A portfolio that tracks its benchmark exactly has spent none of its active risk budget. Given an ex ante active risk budget explicitly provided by the client, the manager instead optimizes the portfolio's exposures relative to the benchmark so that the choices among stocks, sectors, or countries make efficient use of that budget.
rationales.B: Risk budgeting is a process by which the total risk appetite of the portfolio is allocated among the various components of portfolio choice. For example, if the portfolio manager has an ex ante active risk budget explicitly provided by the client, then with risk budgeting she seeks to optimize the portfolio's exposures relative to the benchmark to ensure that the choices she makes among stocks, sectors, or countries make efficient use of the active risk budget. Ex ante active risk is just one possible measure of risk for this purpose.
rationales.C: Risk budgeting explicitly constrains and allocates risk rather than ignoring it in pursuit of return. The total risk appetite of the portfolio is divided among the various components of portfolio choice, and exposures relative to the benchmark are optimized subject to that budget rather than without regard to it.

questions.stem: The first step in an effective equity portfolio risk management process is most likely to:

options.A: apply one absolute risk measure to every strategy.
options.B: determine which risk measure best suits the strategy.
options.C: delegate all risk-allocation decisions to the client.

rationales.A: No single absolute measure can be imposed uniformly. The first step is to determine which type of risk measure is most appropriate to the strategy, and that choice depends on the mandate and the investor's objectives: a long/short equity manager benchmarked against a cash plus target usually prefers an absolute measure such as total volatility of portfolio returns, whereas a long-only manager benchmarked against a capitalization-weighted index may prefer a relative measure such as active risk.
rationales.B: An effective risk management process requires the portfolio manager to do the following: (1) determine which type of risk measure is most appropriate to the strategy; (2) understand how each aspect of the strategy contributes to its overall risk — total portfolio variance may be dominated by exposure to rewarded risk factors or by allocations to countries, sectors, or securities, and if these exposures are dynamic, the timing of portfolio exposures also introduces risk, so an important step in risk budgeting is to understand what drives a portfolio's risk and to ensure the portfolio has the right kinds of specific risks; (3) determine what level of risk budget is appropriate; and (4) properly allocate risk among individual positions and factors. Whether the risk measure is absolute or relative, managers must efficiently allocate their targeted risk budget.
rationales.C: Risk budgeting is the manager's own work. The client sets the mandate and the investment objectives, but the manager must determine which risk measure fits the strategy, understand what drives the portfolio's risk, set the level of the risk budget, and then allocate that budget efficiently among individual positions and factors.

questions.stem: The choice between an absolute and a relative risk measure is most likely:

options.A: dictated by regulation that is identical across jurisdictions.
options.B: determined solely by the benchmark's historical volatility.
options.C: driven by the manager's mandate and the investors' goals.

rationales.A: No uniform body of regulation dictates the orientation, and regulatory regimes are not identical across jurisdictions. The choice is driven by the mandate of the manager and the goals of investors.
rationales.B: Benchmark volatility is an input to estimating risk, not the criterion for choosing the orientation. The choice is driven by the mandate of the manager and the goals of investors: a long-only manager benchmarked against a capitalization-weighted index may prefer a relative measure whatever the index's realized volatility has been.
rationales.C: The choice between an absolute and a relative risk portfolio management orientation is driven by the mandate of the manager and the goals of investors. If the mandate is to outperform a market index over a horizon, such as three years, then the manager will focus on active risk. If the investment objective is expressed in terms of total returns, then the manager will likely focus on the volatility of portfolio returns. So a long/short equity manager benchmarked against a cash plus target will usually prefer an absolute risk measure, such as total volatility of portfolio returns, whereas a long-only equity manager benchmarked against a capitalization-weighted index may prefer a relative risk measure, such as active risk.

questions.stem: An individual asset's contribution to total portfolio variance is most likely:

options.A: equal to its weight times its covariance with the portfolio.
options.B: unrelated to its covariances with the other holdings.
options.C: undefined, since no such decomposition exists.

rationales.A: The contribution of asset i to total portfolio variance is CV_i = Σ x_i × x_j × C_ij = x_i × C_ip, where x_j is the asset's weight in the portfolio, C_ij is the covariance of returns between asset i and asset j, and C_ip is the covariance of returns between asset i and the portfolio. In other words, the contribution of an asset to total portfolio variance is equal to the product of the weight of the asset and its covariance with the entire portfolio, and these contributions sum to total portfolio variance.
rationales.B: Covariance with every other holding is exactly what the summation aggregates: Σ x_i × x_j × C_ij runs over all holdings j and collapses to x_i × C_ip. An asset's variance contribution is therefore a function of its covariance with each of the other positions, and with itself, weighted by their portfolio weights.
rationales.C: The decomposition exists and is exact: CV_i = Σ x_i × x_j × C_ij = x_i × C_ip, the asset's weight times its covariance with the entire portfolio. Summed across holdings, these contributions reproduce total portfolio variance, which is what makes position-level risk budgeting possible.

questions.stem: Asset A makes up 40% of a portfolio, has a return standard deviation of 20%, and has a correlation of 0.88 with the portfolio, whose return standard deviation is 11.9%. Asset A's share of total portfolio variance is most likely:

options.A: indeterminate from the data given.
options.B: greater than its share of portfolio weight.
options.C: undefined for an individual holding.

rationales.A: The share is fully determined by the figures given. An asset's contribution to total portfolio variance is its weight times its covariance with the portfolio: C_ip = 0.88 × 0.20 × 0.119 = 0.0210, so the contribution is 0.40 × 0.0210 ≈ 0.0084 against total portfolio variance of 0.119² ≈ 0.0142, a share of about 59%.
rationales.B: Asset A's contribution to total portfolio variance is calculated as the weight of Asset A times the weight of each holding times the covariance of that holding with Asset A: 0.40 × 0.40 × 0.04 + 0.40 × 0.50 × 0.0096 + 0.40 × 0.10 × 0.0024 = 0.008416. The proportion of total portfolio variance contributed by Asset A is therefore 0.008416/0.014212 = 59.22%. Asset A, which has an allocation of 40%, accounts for nearly 60% of total portfolio variance. This is not surprising, because the correlation of Asset A with the portfolio is 0.88 and its 20% volatility is well above the portfolio's 11.9%: equivalently, 0.40 × (0.88 × 0.20 × 0.119)/0.0142 ≈ 59%. Asset B contributes 39.35% of total portfolio variance and Asset C contributes 1.44%, so risk share and capital share diverge sharply across the three holdings.
rationales.C: Contribution to variance is well defined for a single holding: CV_i = Σ x_i × x_j × C_ij = x_i × C_ip, the asset's weight times its covariance with the portfolio. Here that gives 0.008416 for Asset A, or 0.008416/0.014212 = 59.22% of total portfolio variance, with Asset B at 39.35% and Asset C at 1.44%; the three shares sum to the whole.

questions.stem: In an absolute risk factor attribution of a broad market index, a value index, and an actively managed value fund, the fund's attribution most likely shows:

options.A: no measurable factor exposures.
options.B: no comparable attribution for the indexes.
options.C: a larger unexplained share of risk than either index.

rationales.A: The fund's absolute risk does decompose into factor exposures: market 57.7%, size 1.8%, value 18.1% and momentum −3.5%, which together explain 74.1% of a total absolute risk of 18.0%. The factors are measurable; what is distinctive is how much risk they leave unexplained.
rationales.B: Both indexes are attributed on the same basis as the fund. The Russell 1000 Index shows market 100.4%, size −1.8%, value 0.2%, momentum 0.5%, total explained 99.3%, total unexplained 0.7% and total absolute risk 14.5%. The Russell 1000 Value Index shows market 88.9%, size −1.6%, value 12.5%, momentum −5.2%, total explained 94.6%, total unexplained 5.4% and total absolute risk 14.2%. The comparison with the fund is the point of the attribution.
rationales.C: Value Fund: market 57.7%, size 1.8%, value 18.1%, momentum −3.5%, total explained 74.1%, total unexplained 25.9%, total absolute risk 18.0%. Against that, the Russell 1000 Index shows market 100.4%, size −1.8%, value 0.2%, momentum 0.5%, total explained 99.3%, total unexplained 0.7%, total absolute risk 14.5%; and the Russell 1000 Value Index shows market 88.9%, size −1.6%, value 12.5%, momentum −5.2%, total explained 94.6%, total unexplained 5.4%, total absolute risk 14.2%. Market exposure alone accounts for essentially all of a broad index's absolute risk, and the rewarded factors account for nearly all of a style index's. The actively managed fund is different in kind: only 74.1% of its risk is explained by the four factors, leaving 25.9% unexplained — the idiosyncratic, stock-specific risk the manager has chosen to take — and its total absolute risk of 18.0% exceeds both benchmarks' 14.5% and 14.2%.

questions.stem: The set of constraints most consistent with a concentrated stock picker is most likely:

options.A: 1% active risk, 3% sector deviation, 1% single-security risk.
options.B: 7% active risk, 15% sector deviation, 3% single-security risk.
options.C: 10% active risk, 0% sector deviation, 5% single-security risk.

rationales.A: This is the closet indexer's profile. The low targeted active risk of 1% combined with the narrow 3% sector deviation constraint and a 1% cap on any single security's contribution to risk indicates that the manager is making very few active bets of any kind — the opposite of a concentrated portfolio.
rationales.B: This is the sector rotator's profile. The significant 7% active risk together with a high tolerance for sector deviations, 15%, and security concentration, 3%, is what one would expect of a manager who expresses views at the sector level. A concentrated stock picker takes no sector deviations at all, which is inconsistent with a 15% sector limit.
rationales.C: A 10% active risk target indicates a willingness to tolerate significant performance deviations from the market, and the 5% limit on a single security's contribution to portfolio risk indicates a willingness to run a concentrated portfolio. The unwillingness to take sector deviations, 0%, combined with the high tolerance for idiosyncratic risk indicates that the manager focuses on stock selection and is therefore a stock picker. For contrast: 1% active risk with a 3% sector deviation and 1% single-security limit is a closet indexer, making very few active bets; 4% active risk with a 10% sector deviation and a 1% single-security limit implies a highly diversified portfolio whose significant sector deviations despite that diversification, along with relatively low tracking error, are indicative of a multi-factor manager; and 7% active risk with a 15% sector deviation and 3% single-security limit is a sector rotator.

questions.stem: A portfolio's active variance is most likely:

options.A: undefined, since no such measure exists.
options.B: qualitative only, with no stated expression.
options.C: a sum of relative-return covariances weighted by active weights.

rationales.A: Active variance has an explicit expression. One measure of relative risk is the variance of the portfolio's active return: AV_p = Σ Σ (x_i − b_i)(x_j − b_j) × RC_ij, where x_i is the asset's weight in the portfolio, b_i is the benchmark weight in asset i, and RC_ij is the covariance of relative returns between asset i and asset j.
rationales.B: The measure is stated precisely, not merely described: AV_p = Σ Σ (x_i − b_i)(x_j − b_j) × RC_ij, and it decomposes by position as well, so each holding's share of active risk can be quantified.
rationales.C: Active variance is the double sum of active-weight cross-products times the covariances of relative returns: AV_p = Σ Σ (x_i − b_i)(x_j − b_j) × RC_ij, where x_i is the asset's weight in the portfolio, b_i is the benchmark weight in asset i, and RC_ij is the covariance of relative returns between asset i and asset j. The contribution of each asset to the portfolio active variance is CAV_i = (x_i − b_i) × RC_ip, where RC_ip is the covariance of relative returns between asset i and the portfolio. Positions held at benchmark weight drop out, since their active weight is zero, which is why relative risk is driven entirely by the pattern of overweights and underweights and by how their relative returns covary.

questions.stem: An active equity manager should most likely:

options.A: take risks related to their perceived skills.
options.B: diversify away the risks tied to their perceived skills.
options.C: maximize exposure to every rewarded factor.

rationales.A: Irrespective of whether a manager focuses on absolute risk or relative risk, the risks chosen should be related to perceived skills; all other risk should be diversified or minimized. Market timers should be concerned with timing their factor exposure, sector rotators should be concerned with timing their sector exposure, and multi-factor managers should be concerned with balancing their factor exposure.
rationales.B: This inverts the principle. The risk aligned with perceived skill is the risk the manager is paid to take and should retain — timing factor exposure for a market timer, timing sector exposure for a sector rotator, balancing factor exposure for a multi-factor manager. It is all the other, incidental risk that should be diversified away or minimized.
rationales.C: The criterion is alignment with perceived skill, not maximal factor exposure. A manager takes the risks related to the skills they believe they have and diversifies or minimizes everything else; loading up on factors the manager has no edge in timing or balancing adds risk without an expected reward from skill.

drills.los_text: discuss risk measures that are incorporated in equity portfolio construction and describe how limits set on these measures affect portfolio construction

questions.stem: Relative to formal risk constraints, heuristic constraints are most likely:

options.A: limits on portfolio characteristics rather than on statistical risk.
options.B: not a distinct category of constraint.
options.C: different in name only.

rationales.A: Heuristic constraints are expressed through portfolio characteristics. Samples used by a portfolio manager include: any single position is limited to the lesser of five times the weight of the security in the benchmark or 2%; the portfolio must have a weighted average capitalization of no less than 75% of that of the index; the portfolio may not size any position such that it exceeds two times the average daily trading volume of the past three months; and the portfolio's carbon footprint must be limited to no more than 75% of the benchmark's exposure. Formal risk measures are distinct from these heuristic controls. They are often statistical in nature and directly linked to the distribution of returns for the portfolio, and they include volatility, active risk, skewness, drawdowns, value at risk (VaR), conditional value at risk (CVaR), incremental value at risk (IVaR) and marginal value at risk (MVaR). Formal measures require the manager to estimate or predict risk, whereas heuristic constraints simply bind observable portfolio characteristics.
rationales.B: The heuristic/formal split organizes the whole discussion of constraints: a cap of the lesser of five times benchmark weight or 2% on a position, or a weighted average capitalization floor of 75% of the index, is a heuristic control, while volatility, active risk, drawdowns and VaR are formal measures linked to the distribution of returns.
rationales.C: The difference is one of substance, not labeling. Heuristic constraints are judgment-based limits on observable portfolio characteristics — position size, average capitalization, trading volume, carbon footprint — and can be checked directly from the holdings. Formal constraints are statistical measures of the return distribution — volatility, active risk, skewness, drawdowns, VaR, CVaR, IVaR, MVaR — and require the manager to estimate or predict risk.

questions.stem: Value at risk (VaR) is most likely:

options.A: the average loss beyond a given threshold.
options.B: a term with no standard definition.
options.C: the minimum loss expected a given percentage of the time.

rationales.A: The average of the losses in the tail beyond the threshold is conditional value at risk (CVaR), a separate formal risk measure. VaR itself is the threshold: the minimum loss that would be expected a certain percentage of the time over a specific period of time, given the modeled market conditions.
rationales.B: VaR is defined precisely: the minimum loss that would be expected a certain percentage of the time over a specific period of time, such as a day, a week or a month, given the modeled market conditions.
rationales.C: VaR is the minimum loss that would be expected a certain percentage of the time over a specific period of time — for example, a day, a week or a month — given the modeled market conditions. It is typically expressed as the minimum loss that can be expected to occur 5% of the time. It sits among the formal, statistical risk measures linked to the distribution of portfolio returns, alongside volatility, active risk, skewness, drawdowns, conditional value at risk (CVaR), incremental value at risk (IVaR) and marginal value at risk (MVaR).

questions.stem: Conditional VaR (CVaR) is most likely the:

options.A: maximum loss that could ever be incurred over the investment horizon.
options.B: minimum loss expected a certain percentage of the time over a period.
options.C: average loss incurred if the VaR cutoff is exceeded.

rationales.A: CVaR is the average loss beyond the VaR cutoff, not the absolute worst-case loss. No measure in the VaR family reports a maximum conceivable loss: VaR states a threshold loss at a stated probability, and CVaR averages the losses that exceed that threshold.
rationales.B: This defines VaR, not CVaR, and confuses the threshold loss with the average tail loss. VaR is the minimum loss that would be expected a certain percentage of the time over a given period; CVaR goes further and averages the losses that occur once that cutoff is breached.
rationales.C: CVaR is the average loss that would be incurred if the VaR cutoff is exceeded. It is also sometimes referred to as the expected tail loss or expected shortfall, and it is not technically a VaR measure: instead of reporting the loss threshold at a stated probability, it summarizes the severity of the losses beyond that threshold.

questions.stem: Incremental VaR (IVaR) is most likely the change in portfolio VaR caused by:

options.A: the same input that marginal VaR captures.
options.B: an input that is not separately defined.
options.C: adding a new position, reducing existing position sizes.

rationales.A: IVaR and marginal VaR are not two names for one measure, and they do not respond to the same input. IVaR measures the VaR change from adding a position to the portfolio; MVaR measures the effect of a very small change in the size of a position already held.
rationales.B: The distinction is drawn explicitly. IVaR is the change in portfolio VaR from adding a new position, while MVaR reflects the effect of a very small change in position size, so the two inputs are separately specified rather than undefined.
rationales.C: IVaR is the change in portfolio VaR when adding a new position to a portfolio, thereby reducing the position size of current positions. MVaR, by contrast, reflects the effect of a very small change in the position size. In a diversified portfolio, marginal VaR may be used to determine the contribution of each asset to the overall VaR.

questions.stem: Volatility is most likely the:

options.A: standard deviation of portfolio returns less benchmark returns.
options.B: standard deviation of portfolio returns.
options.C: average absolute deviation of returns from the risk-free rate.

rationales.A: That describes active risk, also called tracking error or tracking risk: the standard deviation of the differences between a portfolio's returns and its benchmark's returns. It is commonly confused with total volatility, but it measures the variability of relative return rather than of the portfolio's return itself.
rationales.B: Volatility is the standard deviation of portfolio returns. Active risk is the standard deviation of the differences between a portfolio's returns and its benchmark's returns, and is also called tracking error or tracking risk. Skewness measures the degree to which return expectations are non-normally distributed: a positively skewed distribution has a mean greater than its median, while negative skew indicates that the mean lies below the median and that the average magnitude of negative deviations is larger than the average magnitude of positive deviations. Drawdown measures the portfolio loss from its high point until it begins to recover.
rationales.C: Volatility is a standard deviation, not a mean absolute deviation, and it is measured around the portfolio's own mean return rather than against the risk-free rate.

questions.stem: A risk report comparing three active equity managers is most likely to present:

options.A: absolute risk only.
options.B: no quantified risk measures.
options.C: absolute risk, active risk, VaR, and CVaR.

rationales.A: Absolute risk is not reported on its own: active risk, VaR, and CVaR at both the 5% and 1% levels appear alongside it. A factor-diversified manager with 10.89% absolute risk also shows 3.4% active risk, 1.08% VaR at 5%, and 1.50% CVaR at 5%.
rationales.B: Risk measures are quantified for all three managers. Absolute risk, active risk, VaR, and CVaR are each tabulated, which is what makes a side-by-side comparison of the managers possible.
rationales.C: A comparison of this kind reports absolute risk, active risk, VaR, and CVaR together. Manager A (factor diversified): absolute risk 10.89%, active risk 3.4%, VaR (5%) 1.08%, VaR (1%) 1.77%, CVaR (5%) 1.50%, CVaR (1%) 2.21%. Manager B (factor diversified): absolute risk 10.87%, active risk 3.6%, VaR (5%) 1.11%, VaR (1%) 1.77%, CVaR (5%) 1.53%, CVaR (1%) 2.24%. Manager C (sector rotator): absolute risk 11.69%, active risk 4.5%, VaR (5%) 1.20%, VaR (1%) 1.87%, CVaR (5%) 1.65%, CVaR (1%) 2.41%. The measures are read together: Manager A has a 5% probability of realizing a one-day loss greater than 1.08% and a 1% probability of a loss greater than 1.77%, while the sector rotator carries both the higher absolute risk and the higher active risk of the three.

questions.stem: For a diversified multi-factor index built by optimizing factor exposure, constituent and sector weights are most likely:

options.A: capped at the greater of two points above or ten times the parent weight; sectors within five percent.
options.B: uncapped against the parent weight, with sectors limited to ten percent.
options.C: capped at ten points above the parent weight, with sectors unconstrained.

rationales.A: The weight of an index constituent is capped at the maximum of its weight in the parent (capitalization-weighted) index plus 2%, or 10 times its weight in the parent index. Sector weights are restricted to a 5% deviation against the parent index, exposure to style factors such as growth and liquidity is restricted to a 0.25 standard deviation from the parent index, and volatility is likewise restricted to a 0.25 standard deviation from the parent index. The index reaches these targets through an optimization process that maximizes the exposure score to several risk factors while controlling those portfolio and risk characteristics.
rationales.B: Constituent weights are explicitly constrained, at the maximum of the parent index weight plus 2% or 10 times the parent index weight, so they are not left uncapped. Sector weights are restricted to a 5% deviation against the parent index, not 10%.
rationales.C: The constituent cap is the maximum of the parent index weight plus 2% or 10 times the parent index weight, not the parent weight plus 10%. Sector weights are also constrained, to a 5% deviation against the parent index, rather than left unconstrained.

questions.stem: When a two-times levered portfolio of highly rated mortgage-related securities suffered a steep price decline in 2008, the result was most likely:

options.A: gradual losses spread over several years.
options.B: a total loss of capital in a forced liquidation.
options.C: a full recovery after holding through the decline.

rationales.A: The securities were highly rated and were not materially exposed to subprime mortgages, and their prices quickly recovered rather than declining permanently. The loss was also sudden rather than gradual: it was crystallized in a forced liquidation within days, not accumulated over several years.
rationales.B: In 2008 a hedge fund owned a two-times levered portfolio of highly rated mortgage-related securities. Although the specific securities were not materially exposed to subprime mortgages, concerns about the economy and poor market liquidity led to a steep decline in the prices of these securities. Prices quickly recovered, but the presence of the 2x leverage combined with an unprecedented price decline led to a forced liquidation of the assets just a few days before prices recovered, and the manager and his investors lost all capital. The consequences of being wrong about risk expectations can be significant, and they are more significant still when the strategy is leveraged.
rationales.C: Holding through the decline was not possible. The 2x leverage, combined with an unprecedented price decline, forced liquidation of the assets just a few days before prices recovered, so the manager and his investors lost all capital despite the recovery in prices.

questions.stem: The realized volatility of the S&P 500 between 1995 and 2020 is most likely:

options.A: constant throughout the period.
options.B: range bound most of the time, with episodes of far higher levels.
options.C: unvarying from year to year.

rationales.A: Volatility is time varying, not constant. It remains in a range of 10% to 20% most of the time, but periods of much higher volatility are observed: 2000-2002, when technology stocks collapsed, 2008-2009, during the Global Financial Crisis, and 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic.
rationales.B: Volatility remains in a range of 10% to 20% most of the time, but periods of much higher volatility are observed: in 2000-2002 when technology stocks collapsed, in 2008-2009 during the Global Financial Crisis, and in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Effective risk management requires the manager to account for the fact that unexpected volatility can derail the investment strategy. Spikes in volatility can also be sector specific, as in the technology sector in the early 2000s and the energy sector in 2014 and 2015, so what may seem an acceptable sector deviation limit in normal times may be the source of significant active losses in a different environment. Some managers tighten risk constraints in more volatile periods to protect the portfolio against excessive variability.
rationales.C: The variation is the central feature of the record: long stretches inside a 10% to 20% range, interrupted by episodes of far higher volatility in 2000-2002, 2008-2009, and 2020.
