drills.los_text: discuss how assets under management, position size, market liquidity, and portfolio turnover affect equity portfolio construction decisions

questions.stem: Market impact is most likely:

options.A: a fixed per-share cost, independent of trade size and liquidity.
options.B: a concern only for high-turnover strategies demanding immediacy.
options.C: a price movement caused by the manager's own trade that erodes alpha.

rationales.A: Market impact is a function of the liquidity and trade size of the security, so it is not a fixed cost per share. The same order moves the price of a thinly traded security far more than it moves the price of a liquid one, and a larger order moves either price more than a smaller one.
rationales.B: Every manager is exposed to market impact; turnover and immediacy change its size, not its existence. A strategy that demands immediacy in execution or requires higher portfolio turnover is likely to incur higher market impact costs than a manager who patiently trades into a position, and a manager who believes her insights will be rewarded over a longer-term horizon can mitigate market impact by slowly building up positions as liquidity becomes available, but she does not escape it.
rationales.C: The price movement, or market impact, resulting from a manager's purchase or sale of a security can materially erode the manager's alpha. Market impact is a function of the liquidity and trade size of the security, and a manager's investment approach and style influence the extent to which he is exposed to it: a manager whose strategy demands immediacy in execution or requires higher portfolio turnover is likely to incur higher market impact costs relative to a manager who patiently trades into a position. A manager who believes her investment insights will be rewarded over a longer-term investment horizon may be able to mitigate market impact costs by slowly building up positions as liquidity becomes available.

questions.stem: A trade that contains information is most likely to:

options.A: convey no signal to other market participants.
options.B: leave execution prices unaffected.
options.C: signal likely price pressure as the position is built.

rationales.A: A trade contains information when the manager's decision to buy or sell signals to the market that something has changed, and visible accumulation by a discretionary manager with sizable assets under management is exactly such a signal: it tells other participants that there is likely to be upward pressure on the price as the position is built.
rationales.B: The signal moves execution prices against the informed trader. Some market participants may try to front-run the manager, buying up known supply in order to sell it to the manager at a higher price, which raises the cost of completing the position.
rationales.C: If a discretionary manager with sizable assets under management begins to buy a stock, the trade signals to other market participants that there is likely to be upward pressure on the stock price as the manager builds the position. Some market participants may try to front-run the manager, buying up known supply to sell it to the manager at a higher price. If that same manager begins to sell his position following a company event, it signals to the market that the manager's view on the stock has changed and that he is likely to be selling off the position, putting downward pressure on the price. A manager whose trades contain information is therefore more vulnerable to market impact costs.

questions.stem: Among the constituents of the Russell 1000 Index, the capitalization and trading data most likely show:

options.A: capitalization skewed, with the average declining quickly down the list.
options.B: capitalization spread evenly across large and small constituents.
options.C: smaller companies trading a smaller share of their capitalization daily.

rationales.A: Two observations are warranted. First, the distribution of market cap is skewed: average capitalization declines quickly, and the combined capitalization of the top 500 companies is more than seven times that of the bottom 500 companies. Second, smaller-capitalization companies have lower daily trading volume in dollars, yet they trade a greater percentage of their capitalization: the smallest 900 companies within the index trade nearly two times more volume, as a percentage of their market capitalization, than the 100 largest companies, averaging about 1% of market cap daily against 0.5% for the 100 largest. Nevertheless, the lower absolute level of average trading volume of the smaller securities can be a significant implementation hurdle for a manager running a strategy with significant assets under management and significant positive active weights on smaller companies.
rationales.B: The distribution is skewed rather than even. Average capitalization declines quickly, and the combined capitalization of the top 500 companies is more than seven times that of the bottom 500 companies, so the two halves of the index are nothing like comparable in size.
rationales.C: This inverts the finding. Smaller-capitalization companies have lower daily trading volume in dollars but trade a greater percentage of their capitalization: the smallest 900 companies average about 1% of their market cap traded daily, against 0.5% for the 100 largest, which is nearly twice as much in percentage terms.

questions.stem: A manager with $200 million under management limits any position to 2% of total assets and to 10% of a security's average daily trading volume. For a security with a $2 billion market capitalization of which 1% trades on an average day, the position size is most likely:

options.A: limited by the liquidity policy.
options.B: not determinable from the policies given.
options.C: unconstrained by either policy.

rationales.A: Both policies apply and the tighter one governs. The allocation limit permits $200 million × 2% = $4 million of the security. The liquidity policy permits 10% of average daily volume, and average daily volume is 1% of the $2 billion capitalization, or about $20 million, so $20 million × 10% = $2 million. The liquidity limit of $2 million therefore binds first, holding the position to roughly 1.0% of fund assets rather than the 2% the allocation limit would allow. The same constraint falls much harder on larger funds: a $1 billion fund operating under identical policies is still limited to the same $2 million position, a far smaller position relative to its total assets.
rationales.B: The position size is fully determinable from the two policies: $200 million × 2% = $4 million under the allocation limit, and 10% of the $20 million average daily volume = $2 million under the liquidity limit. Nothing further is needed; the smaller of the two figures, $2 million, is the maximum position.
rationales.C: Neither policy is slack. The liquidity policy caps the position at $2 million, being 10% of the roughly $20 million that trades on an average day, and that cap binds before the $4 million allowed by the 2% allocation limit, so the position is constrained to about 1.0% of the fund's assets.

questions.stem: A large-AUM fund addressing the liquidity constraints of its strategy is most likely to:

options.A: set position limits scaled to each security's market-cap weight.
options.B: close the fund to new investors as its only remedy.
options.C: have no mechanism available for managing liquidity.

rationales.A: A large-AUM fund has several structural levers. It can set position limits on individual securities that reference each security's market-cap weight on both an absolute and a relative basis — for example, limiting the allocation to the lesser of market-cap weight plus 1% (100 bps) or 10 times the security's market-cap weight in the index, so that the limit is tied to each security's market capitalization. It can set position limits based on average daily trading volume — for example, no more than 10 days of average trading volume. And it can build a rebalancing strategy into the investment process that anticipates a longer rebalancing period, or that rebalances gradually and consistently over time, assuming the strategy's performance is not impaired by the implementation delay.
rationales.B: Closing the fund is one lever among several, not the only remedy. The primary tools are structural: position limits tied to market-cap weight, position limits tied to days of average trading volume, and a longer or more gradual rebalancing schedule.
rationales.C: Mechanisms are available. Position limits scaled to market capitalization and to average daily trading volume, liquidity-aware position sizing, and a lengthened or more gradual rebalancing process all let a large fund manage the constraint.

questions.stem: Compared with large-cap funds, small-cap funds most likely:

options.A: face no distinctive implementation issues.
options.B: draw on benchmarks free of very small-capitalization constituents.
options.C: face tighter capacity and liquidity constraints.

rationales.A: Small-cap investing raises distinctive capacity and liquidity problems. The weighted average capitalization of the Russell 2000 Index is only about $2.2 billion, so positions constrained by trading volume are small in absolute terms and a concentrated strategy can struggle to deploy even $100 million.
rationales.B: Nearly 60% of Russell 2000 constituents have a market capitalization below $1 billion, so the small-cap benchmark is dominated by companies whose limited capitalization and trading volume create the constraint in the first place.
rationales.C: Capacity and liquidity constraints bind far more tightly in small caps. The weighted average capitalization of the Russell 2000 Index is only about $2.2 billion, and nearly 60% of its companies have a market capitalization below $1 billion. A small-cap manager working under the same 10%-of-average-daily-volume limit would have an average position of no more than about $2.5 million. A strategy rooted in a smaller number of securities — say, 40 — may therefore find it difficult to run a $100 million fund, and may have to concentrate its allocation among the largest 25% of index securities or accept lower turnover. A strategy holding more securities — say, 200 — can support substantially higher AUM but may still be constrained toward the larger, more liquid names, and small-cap funds with capacity of $1 billion or greater may need to hold 400 securities or more.

questions.stem: Slippage is most likely:

options.A: measured against the bid-ask midpoint when the order was entered.
options.B: not measurable as a trading cost.
options.C: unrelated to the prices at which trades execute.

rationales.A: Slippage is often measured as the difference between the execution price and the midpoint of the bid and ask quotes at the time the trade was first entered. Measured that way it incorporates both volatility/trend costs — the costs associated with buying into a rising market and selling into a declining one — and market impact. It provides an estimate of the cost of executing a transaction when the order is executed in a single trade.
rationales.B: It is measured routinely, as the execution price against the midpoint of the bid and ask quotes prevailing when the trade was first entered, and that measure captures both volatility/trend costs and market impact.
rationales.C: Execution prices are the whole of the measure: slippage is the realized execution price relative to the quote midpoint at order entry, so it is defined by the prices at which trades execute.

questions.stem: Across equity markets, slippage costs most likely:

options.A: matter less than commission costs.
options.B: matter more than commission costs.
options.C: are larger for large-cap securities and stable over time.

rationales.A: The ordering runs the other way. Estimates of average slippage across markets support the conclusion that slippage costs are usually more important than commission costs, with commissions the smaller component of total trading cost.
rationales.B: Three conclusions follow from estimates of average slippage across markets: slippage costs are usually more important than commission costs; slippage costs are greater for smaller-cap securities than for large-cap securities; and slippage costs can vary substantially over time, especially when market volatility is higher.
rationales.C: Both halves of this are reversed. Slippage costs are greater for smaller-cap securities than for large-cap securities, and they are not stable — they can vary substantially over time, especially when market volatility is higher.

questions.stem: Unlit venues such as dark pools and crossing networks most likely:

options.A: serve only retail order flow.
options.B: let buyers and sellers trade anonymously.
options.C: require full pre-trade disclosure of order size.

rationales.A: These venues are used chiefly by large institutional investors seeking to trade big blocks anonymously; they are not retail-only venues, and concealing institutional block size is their main purpose.
rationales.B: Unlit venues allow buyers and sellers to trade anonymously with one another, and dark pools and crossing networks are the standard examples. Large institutional investors often try to camouflage the potential size of a trade either by breaking it into many smaller trades or by trading in unlit venues. One reason is that when a larger trade is executed in increments over multiple days, the estimate of market impact cost for the later trades does not account for the effect earlier trades have already had on subsequent execution prices. An institution wanting to sell a big block without alerting other participants to the pending activity can instead trade anonymously in these private venues, where transactions are completed in the dark, without full transparency — a practice that has become a powerful force in financial markets.
rationales.C: Transactions in unlit venues are completed without full transparency, and that opacity is precisely why institutions use them: pre-trade disclosure of order size would alert other participants to the pending activity the institution is trying to conceal.

drills.los_text: evaluate the efficiency of a portfolio structure given its investment mandate

questions.stem: A well-constructed active equity portfolio most likely exhibits:

options.A: the lowest attainable Active Share.
options.B: risk exposures aligned with investor expectations and constraints.
options.C: high idiosyncratic risk relative to total risk.

rationales.A: When other factors are equal, a higher Active Share is preferable rather than a lower one, because it leverages the manager's alpha skills and carries higher expected returns; minimizing Active Share would suppress the very skill the investor is paying for.
rationales.B: In a well-constructed portfolio we look for risk exposures aligned with investor expectations and constraints, together with low idiosyncratic (unexplained) risk relative to total risk. If two products have comparable factor exposures, the product with lower absolute volatility and lower active risk will likely be preferred, assuming similar costs. If two products have similar active and absolute risks, similar costs, and managers of similar alpha skill, the product with the higher Active Share is preferable, because it leverages the manager's alpha skills and will have higher expected returns.
rationales.C: A well-constructed portfolio shows low idiosyncratic, unexplained risk relative to total risk. High unexplained risk indicates exposures the investor did not intend and did not expect to be paid for.

questions.stem: The risk efficiency of a given portfolio approach is most appropriately judged:

options.A: in the context of the investor's total portfolio.
options.B: on each mandate in isolation.
options.C: by comparing managers' information ratios alone.

rationales.A: The risk efficiency of any given portfolio approach should be judged in the context of the investor's total portfolio. The active risk of a concentrated stock picker should be higher than that of a diversified factor investor, and the concentrated stock picker may have a lower information ratio, yet both managers could be building a well-structured portfolio relative to their own mandate. It is important to consider the diversification effect of a manager's portfolio on the total portfolio of the investor in order to arrive at an appropriate solution.
rationales.B: Judging each mandate in isolation ignores the diversification effect of a manager's portfolio on the investor's total portfolio, which is exactly the consideration needed to arrive at an appropriate solution.
rationales.C: A concentrated stock picker may carry a lower information ratio than a diversified factor investor and still be running a well-structured portfolio relative to its mandate, so the information ratio on its own does not settle risk efficiency.

questions.stem: Product A has a market beta slightly below 1, a negative Size coefficient, a very large Value exposure and about 320 holdings; Product B has balanced factor exposures with a large Quality tilt, about 120 holdings and an Active Share nearly double Product A's. Relative to Product B, Product A is most likely:

options.A: more diversified at the security level and more concentrated in one factor.
options.B: equivalent on every dimension evaluated.
options.C: impossible to compare on factor exposures.

rationales.A: Product A's relevant characteristics are a market beta slightly less than 1; a large-cap bias, shown by a negative coefficient on the Size factor; a very large exposure to the Value factor; greater security-level diversification than Product B, at roughly 320 holdings; market risk representing only 87.4% of total portfolio risk; and a significant portion of absolute risk attributed to the Value factor. Product B's are a market beta slightly more than 1; a more balanced exposure to all factors; a large exposure to the Quality factor, although that factor itself has relatively low volatility; an Active Share nearly double Product A's, 0.80 against 0.43; modestly lower drawdowns; roughly 120 holdings; and more than 100% of its absolute risk attributed to the market factor. Product B's emphasis on quality companies — high return on equity, low debt-to-equity ratio, low earnings variability — is a likely explanation for absolute and relative risk measures that are not significantly different from Product A's despite holding less than half as many securities, which indicates that risk management is an important component of Product B's portfolio construction process. There is no guarantee that a more efficiently risk-structured portfolio will outperform, but Product B outperformed Product A by more than 3.1% annually over the period.
rationales.B: The two products differ on nearly every dimension evaluated: market beta either side of 1, the sign and size of the Size and Value loadings, the Quality tilt, Active Share of 0.43 against 0.80, roughly 320 holdings against 120, drawdowns, and the share of absolute risk coming from the market factor — 87.4% of total risk for Product A against more than 100% for Product B.
rationales.C: The products are directly comparable: factor loadings, Active Share, holdings counts, drawdowns and risk decompositions are all measurable for each, and that comparison is the substance of evaluating the two construction approaches.

questions.stem: Larrabee specifies a custom low-volatility, high-payout-yield portfolio to serve as the core of a client's global equity allocation. The investable universe is most likely:

options.A: the Russell 2000 Index.
options.B: the MSCI World Index.
options.C: the S&P 500 Index.

rationales.A: The Russell 2000 is a US small-cap universe, inconsistent both with a global core allocation and with a low-volatility objective that tends toward large-cap names. The universe specified is the securities within the MSCI World Index.
rationales.B: The main specifications for the custom portfolio are an investable universe composed of securities within the MSCI World Index; low volatility achieved through an optimization process; high payout yield, counting both dividends and share repurchases; no fewer than 250 securities; no position greater than 2%; and average portfolio turnover of less than 50% annually. A broad global large-cap universe such as the MSCI World Index fits a portfolio intended as the core of a global equity allocation. Larrabee also understands that a low-volatility objective of this kind usually leads to portfolios carrying large-cap, Value and Quality biases.
rationales.C: The S&P 500 is a US large-cap universe. The specification names the securities within the MSCI World Index, which is global in scope as the client's global equity allocation requires.

questions.stem: A custom global equity portfolio reports an 8.45% annualized return, 9.0% annualized volatility, 325 securities, 35% turnover, and a 3.6% dividend yield, while its MSCI World benchmark reports 2.4% turnover and a 2.6% dividend yield. The benchmark's return, volatility, and security count profile is closest to:

options.A: 7.0% return, 20.0% volatility, 500 securities.
options.B: 8.45% return, 9.0% volatility, 325 securities.
options.C: 7.0% return, 11.3% volatility, 1,700 securities.

rationales.A: The benchmark's volatility is 11.3%, not 20.0%; its security count is roughly 1,700, not 500; and the turnover and yield given in the stem for the benchmark, 2.4% and 2.6%, are consistent with that broad, low-maintenance index rather than with a 500-stock, 15% turnover, 1.5% yield portfolio. A broad developed-market benchmark holds well over a thousand names and turns over only a few percent a year, because constituents change only as the index is reconstituted, and its annualized volatility over the period was 11.3%, well below 20%.
rationales.B: These are the custom portfolio's own figures - 8.45% annualized return, 9.0% annualized volatility, 325 securities, 35% turnover, and a 3.6% dividend yield, carrying 6.0% active risk - mistakenly attributed to the MSCI World benchmark. The stem already assigns them to the portfolio. The portfolio holds roughly one-fifth as many names as the index, turns over more than ten times as fast, and tilts toward higher-yielding stocks, which is precisely why its profile cannot also be the benchmark's.
rationales.C: MSCI World shows a 7.0% annualized return, 11.3% annualized volatility, 1,700 securities, 2.4% turnover, and a 2.6% dividend yield. The custom portfolio shows an 8.45% annualized return, 9.0% annualized volatility, 6.0% active risk, 325 securities, 35% turnover, and a 3.6% dividend yield. Its average active sector exposures are negative in energy (-2.00%), materials (-1.50%), and industrials (-1.50%) and positive in consumer discretionary (+3.00%), consumer staples (+4.20%), and health care (+2.40%). The benchmark is the broad, diversified leg of that comparison: many names, minimal turnover, and a market-level yield and volatility. The custom portfolio concentrates into 325 of those names, which raises turnover to 35% and the yield to 3.6% and generates 6.0% of active risk, yet total volatility falls to 9.0% because the sector tilts away from energy, materials, and industrials and toward staples and health care lower the portfolio's market sensitivity.

questions.stem: Larrabee reviews a simulated core equity mandate that represents 65% of a client's equity allocation and carries 6% active risk, a large underweight to the information technology sector, a positive average excess return over the past 12 years, and negative alpha. Her most likely conclusion is that:

options.A: the tracking error is immaterial.
options.B: the active risk is too high for the allocation.
options.C: the excess return came from stock selection.

rationales.A: The tracking error is material, and the significant under-allocation to information technology contributes to it rather than reducing it: a persistent sector underweight is itself an active position, and active positions add to active risk. With 6% active risk applied to 65% of the total equity allocation, the mandate's contribution to overall tracking error is large enough to pose a problem, so it cannot be dismissed as immaterial.
rationales.B: Six percent active risk on 65% of the equity allocation may be too high; given the size of that allocation relative to the total equity portfolio, it poses a problem. Some of the tracking error may be attributed to the significant under-allocation to the information technology sector. In addition, although the portfolio would have generated a positive excess return on average over the past 12 years, the alpha is negative. Understanding the source of that negative alpha is essential: in this instance the excess return was achieved largely through very high and intentional exposure to rewarded factors such as Value, betting against beta, and Quality, which may not have been rewarded over the simulated period.
rationales.C: The simulated alpha is negative, not positive, so there is no positive alpha to confirm anything. The excess return was achieved largely through very high and intentional exposure to rewarded factors - Value, betting against beta, and Quality - rather than through stock selection, and those factors may not have been rewarded over the simulated period. Negative alpha alongside a positive excess return is the signature of factor exposure doing the work, which is why understanding the source of the negative alpha is essential.

questions.stem: Larrabee's core equity mandate shows a significant negative alpha, an excess return strongly explained by exposure to specific factors, a persistent information technology underweight, and tracking error the client considers high. Her most appropriate first recommendation is to:

options.A: match the benchmark's information technology weight.
options.B: investigate the source of the negative alpha.
options.C: hire satellite managers correlated with the core.

rationales.A: The objective is not necessarily to maintain a technology exposure equal to that of the MSCI World Index, but perhaps to lower the consistent underexposure to a more reasonable level. Eliminating the underweight entirely would discard an intentional active position and would not address the mandate's real problem, which is the negative alpha. At the very least, these structural biases should be continuously monitored rather than mechanically neutralized.
rationales.B: The first recommendation is to investigate further the source of the significant negative alpha. Because the excess performance is so strongly explained by exposure to specific factors, there is reason for concern about how the portfolio would perform if factor returns were to decline, and the question is whether a systemic reason explains the observation. Second, if tracking error is a concern, it is important to identify satellite managers whose active returns have a low correlation with the core mandate, perhaps even a lower active risk. Finally, considering the importance of the information technology sector, it could be prudent to hire a manager with a strong technology orientation. The objective is not necessarily to maintain a technology exposure equal to that of the MSCI World Index but perhaps to lower the consistent underexposure to a more reasonable level, and at the very least these structural biases should be continuously monitored.
rationales.C: Because tracking error is a concern, the recommendation runs the other way: identify satellite managers whose active returns have a low correlation with the core mandate, perhaps even a lower active risk. Hiring managers whose active returns are highly correlated with the core would reinforce the existing factor tilts and add to active risk rather than diversify it, worsening the very problem the client has raised.

questions.stem: An analyst compares active equity managers on active risk, Active Share, average sector deviation, and the share of active risk explained by the market factor. The pairing of manager type with risk profile that is most likely correct is:

options.A: Factor diversified: 4.5% active risk, 0.87 Active Share, 69.2% market factor.
options.B: Factor diversified: 3.4% active risk, 0.76 Active Share, 98.0% market factor.
options.C: Sector rotator: 3.6% active risk, 0.63 Active Share, 99.2% market factor.

rationales.A: Those figures belong to the concentrated sector rotator, not to a factor-diversified manager: 4.5% active risk, 0.87 Active Share, 5.6% average sector deviation, and sources of risk of 69.2% market, 11.6% sectors, 9.7% styles, and 9.5% unexplained. A factor-diversified manager instead shows 3.4% active risk, 0.76 Active Share, 3.6% average sector deviation, and 98.0% of risk explained by the market factor, with sectors at -0.8%, styles at 1.8%, and only 1.0% unexplained. An Active Share of 0.87 combined with barely two-thirds of risk coming from the market is the profile of a concentrated manager taking deliberate sector and style bets.
rationales.B: The factor-diversified manager shows 3.4% active risk, 0.76 Active Share, 3.6% average sector deviation, and sources of risk of 98.0% market, -0.8% sectors, 1.8% styles, and 1.0% unexplained. A second factor-diversified manager shows 3.6% active risk, 0.63 Active Share, 3.9% average sector deviation, and 99.2% market, -3.8% sectors, 4.2% styles, and 0.4% unexplained. The concentrated sector rotator shows 4.5% active risk, 0.87 Active Share, 5.6% average sector deviation, and 69.2% market, 11.6% sectors, 9.7% styles, and 9.5% unexplained, holding 21 positions with the top five at 25.1% and 21.3% in cash and bonds. The consistent pattern is that factor-diversified managers run lower active risk, lower Active Share, and smaller sector deviations, and have nearly all of their active risk explained by the market factor, whereas a sector rotator's sector and style bets and security-specific concentration pull the market share of risk down and push the unexplained share up.
rationales.C: A profile of 3.6% active risk, 0.63 Active Share, 3.9% average sector deviation, and 99.2% market risk belongs to the other factor-diversified manager, with sectors at -3.8%, styles at 4.2%, and 0.4% unexplained. A sector rotator cannot look like that: taking deliberate sector bets drives the sector contribution to risk up, to 11.6%, and the market share down, to 69.2%, alongside 4.5% active risk, 0.87 Active Share, 5.6% average sector deviation, 9.7% styles, and 9.5% unexplained, from a concentrated book of 21 securities with the top five at 25.1%, 21.3% in cash and bonds, a market beta of 1.28, and absolute risk of 11.69%.

questions.stem: A manager holds 21 securities with the top five at 25.1% of the portfolio and 21.3% in cash and bonds, a weighted average capitalization close to that of the index, a market beta of 1.28, absolute risk of 11.69% against an index level only slightly lower, 4.5% active risk, an Active Share of 0.87, an average sector deviation of 5.6%, and 69.2% of active risk explained by the market factor. The most likely interpretation of this profile is that:

options.A: the cash holding pushes absolute risk above the level implied by beta.
options.B: the concentrated holdings indicate a benchmark-aware closet indexer.
options.C: the cash holding dampens portfolio volatility.

rationales.A: The cash position works in the opposite direction: it dampens volatility. A market beta of 1.28 on its own would imply absolute risk well above the index's, yet measured absolute risk is 11.69%, only slightly higher than the index's, and the 21.3% cash and bond position is the most likely reason the gap is so small. Cash has no market exposure, so holding more than a fifth of the portfolio in cash and bonds pulls realized volatility below what the beta of the equity sleeve alone would produce.
rationales.B: The profile is the opposite of a closet indexer's. Twenty-one holdings with the top five at 25.1% is very concentrated and carries high security-specific risk; an Active Share of 0.87 is high and consistent with that concentration; an average sector deviation of 5.6% is high and consistent with a willingness to take sector bets; and only 69.2% of active risk is explained by the market factor, with 11.6% from sectors, 9.7% from styles, and 9.5% unexplained. A closet indexer would show low Active Share, small sector deviations, and almost all of its active risk explained by the market factor.
rationales.C: The large cash position dampens overall portfolio volatility. Read as a whole, the measures line up: the weighted average capitalization of $164.0 billion is much closer to the capitalization of the index; the market beta of 1.28 is significantly higher, consistent with the absolute risk measures; absolute risk of 11.69% is only slightly higher than the index's, likely dampened by the large 21.3% cash and bond position; active risk of 4.5% is higher; the Active Share of 0.87 is high, consistent with the level of security concentration across just 21 names with the top five at 25.1%; and the average sector deviation of 5.6% is higher, consistent with a willingness to take sector bets. The sources of risk show significantly less exposure to the market factor at 69.2%, significantly more sector risk at 11.6%, significantly more style risk at 9.7%, and a significantly higher unexplained proportion at 9.5%. Taken together, these measures indicate a benchmark-agnostic strategy with significant and concentrated security, sector, and style exposures.

drills.los_text: discuss the long-only, long extension, long/short, and equitized market-neutral approaches to equity portfolio construction, including their risks, costs, and effects on potential alphas

questions.stem: Long/short, long extension, and market-neutral approaches all rest on the belief that research insights can be exploited to profit from negative as well as positive views. The most encompassing of the three terms is most likely:

options.A: long/short.
options.B: market neutral.
options.C: long extension.

rationales.A: Long/short is the most encompassing term and can include long extension and market-neutral products. All three approaches are variations on a theme: each is predicated on the belief that research insights can be exploited not only in the pursuit of stocks that are expected to perform well but also to profit from the negative insights gathered during the research process. Most commonly, the term long/short refers to strategies that are relatively unconstrained in the extent to which they can lever both positive and negative insights, which is why the narrower, constrained approaches sit underneath it.
rationales.B: The hierarchy is inverted. Market neutral is one variation within the long/short family, distinguished by construction that drives the portfolio's exposures to a wide variety of risk factors to zero. Long/short is the encompassing term and can include both long extension and market-neutral products as variants.
rationales.C: Long extension is one variation under the long/short umbrella, not the umbrella itself. It is a constrained long/short strategy, typically run at a net exposure of 100% - for example, 130% of capital invested long and 30% short - which makes it narrower than long/short, not broader. Long/short is the most encompassing term and can include both long extension and market-neutral products.

questions.stem: Long extension strategies are most likely:

options.A: constrained long/short strategies that lever insights on losers as well as winners.
options.B: not a recognized category of strategy.
options.C: unlevered portfolios with long positions equal to the capital committed.

rationales.A: Long extension strategies are constrained long/short strategies. The capital committed by the client is invested similarly to the manager's long-only strategy but levered to some extent to exploit the manager's insights on projected losers as well as winners. A typical long extension strategy is constrained to have a net exposure of 100%: for example, 130% of the capital is invested long and 30% of the capital is invested short, for a net exposure of 100%, the same as it would be in a long-only portfolio. That construction lets the manager act on negative research insights while leaving the client's market exposure where a long-only mandate would have put it.
rationales.B: Long extension is a well-defined category: a constrained long/short strategy that exploits short-side insights inside a familiar net-long wrapper, with net exposure typically held at 100% through a structure such as 130% long and 30% short.
rationales.C: The extension is the leverage. A long extension strategy invests more than the committed capital long and funds the excess with short positions - for example, 130% long and 30% short - so that gross exposure exceeds 100% even though net exposure remains at 100%. A portfolio holding long positions equal to capital and nothing short would simply be long only.

questions.stem: In a market-neutral strategy, the portfolio's exposures to a wide variety of risk factors are most likely:

options.A: large and positive.
options.B: left unconstrained.
options.C: zero.

rationales.A: Zero factor exposure is the construction target, not large positive exposure. Returns in a market-neutral portfolio are meant to come from security selection within a factor-neutral book, so deliberately carrying large positive exposures to every major risk factor would describe a factor-tilted long/short or long-only strategy instead.
rationales.B: Market neutrality is defined precisely by the constraint: the portfolio is constructed so that its exposures to a wide variety of risk factors are zero, and it may be neutralized against a wide variety of other risk factors as well. Leaving factor exposures unconstrained is what distinguishes a general long/short strategy from a market-neutral one.
rationales.C: Market-neutral strategies are long/short portfolios constructed in a manner that ensures the portfolio's exposures to a wide variety of risk factors are zero, and these portfolios may in addition be neutralized against a wide variety of other risk factors. Because the systematic exposures are engineered away, whatever return remains is attributable to the manager's security selection rather than to factor or market carry, which is why market neutral is treated as the most tightly constrained member of the long/short family.

questions.stem: The consideration that most likely leads an investor to choose a long-only strategy rather than a long/short strategy is:

options.A: guaranteed market-neutral returns.
options.B: unlimited short-side profit potential.
options.C: long-term risk premiums.

rationales.A: Market-neutral construction is a long/short variation, the opposite of the long-only rationale, and it guarantees nothing: neutralizing factor exposures removes the long-term risk premiums that a long-only investor is trying to capture, leaving only whatever security selection produces.
rationales.B: Short-side profit potential is a benefit of long/short strategies, not a reason to choose long only, and it is not unlimited: a short seller's potential losses are unlimited while its gains are capped at the value of the position. Limited legal liability runs the other way, since a long-only investor's maximum loss has a floor at the amount invested.
rationales.C: Long-term risk premiums must be owned to be captured, which is the first of several considerations likely to influence an investor's choice between long only and some variation of long/short. The others are capacity and scale, where long only offers greater capacity - the MSCI ACWI has a total market capitalization of nearly $65.8 trillion, with the 10 largest companies worth $10.4 trillion as of 30 September 2021; limited legal liability and risk appetite, since a long position's maximum loss is floored at the amount invested while a short seller's potential losses are unlimited; regulatory constraints, as some countries ban short selling and on 18 September 2008 the UK Financial Services Authority temporarily prohibited the short selling of financial companies to protect the integrity of the financial system, with the US Securities and Exchange Commission following suit the next day; transactional complexity; management costs, with long/short hedge funds as of 2021 typically charging fixed fees of about 2% and performance fees of about 20%; and personal ideology.

questions.stem: Regarding equity portfolio construction, the statement that is most likely correct is that:

options.A: long/short position weights are nonnegative and sum to one.
options.B: net exposure is the longs plus the absolute value of the shorts.
options.C: long-only position weights are nonnegative and sum to one.

rationales.A: In the long/short approach, position weights can be negative and the weights are not necessarily constrained to sum to one. Some long/short portfolios may even have aggregate exposure of less than one. Nonnegative weights summing to one describe long-only construction, which is exactly the constraint the long/short approach relaxes in order to express negative insights.
rationales.B: The sum of the longs plus the absolute value of the shorts is the portfolio's gross exposure, not its net exposure. Net exposure is the absolute value of the longs minus the absolute value of the shorts. A 130/30 long extension therefore has net exposure of 100% and gross exposure of 160%, and a market-neutral book with 100% long and 100% short has net exposure of zero and gross exposure of 200%.
rationales.C: In a long-only portfolio construction process, the weights assigned to every asset must be greater than or equal to zero and the weights must sum to one. In the long/short approach, by contrast, position weights can be negative and the weights are not necessarily constrained to sum to one, and some long/short portfolios may even have aggregate exposure of less than one. The absolute value of the longs minus the absolute value of the shorts is the portfolio's net exposure, while the sum of the longs plus the absolute value of the shorts is the portfolio's gross exposure, so the two conventions measure how much market the portfolio carries and how much capital it puts to work.

questions.stem: The gross and net exposures of a long/short equity structure, each as a percentage of capital, are most likely:

options.A: Long only, 100/0: 100% gross, 100% net.
options.B: Long extension, 130/30: 100% gross, 160% net.
options.C: Market neutral, 100/100: 0% gross, 200% net.

rationales.A: Gross exposure is the sum of long and short positions; net exposure is long minus short. A long-only portfolio is long 100 and short 0, so gross exposure is 100 + 0 = 100% and net exposure is 100 - 0 = 100%; cash is 0%. The full set of illustrative long/short structures, stated as a percentage of capital, runs: long only, long 100, short 0, cash 0, gross 100, net 100; 130/30 long extension, long 130, short 30, cash 0, gross 160, net 100; market neutral low risk, long 50, short 50, cash 100, gross 100, net 0; market neutral higher risk, long 100, short 100, cash 100, gross 200, net 0; directional low risk, long 80, short 40, cash 60, gross 120, net 40; net short, long 40, short 100, cash 160, gross 140, net -60. Only the long-only row has gross and net exposure both equal to 100%.
rationales.B: This swaps the two measures. A 130/30 long extension is long 130 and short 30, so gross exposure is 130 + 30 = 160% and net exposure is 130 - 30 = 100% - the figures stated here are reversed. The 160% gross figure is what makes the structure a long extension: the investor keeps full 100% net market exposure while adding 60 percentage points of gross exposure to express security selection on both the long and the short side.
rationales.C: This also reverses the measures. A market-neutral structure that is long 100 and short 100 has gross exposure of 100 + 100 = 200% and net exposure of 100 - 100 = 0%, not 0% gross and 200% net. Net exposure of zero is the defining feature of a market-neutral structure, and gross exposure of 200% is the reason the higher-risk variant carries 100% cash as collateral against the short book.

questions.stem: Relative to a long-only strategy, a benefit of a long/short strategy is most likely the:

options.A: fuller expression of short ideas.
options.B: elimination of market risk in every variant.
options.C: reduction of collateral requirements.

rationales.A: Long/short strategies offer three stated benefits: the ability to more fully express short ideas than under a long-only strategy; efficient use of leverage and of the benefits of diversification; and greater ability to calibrate and control exposure to factors (Market and other rewarded factors), sectors, geography, or any undesired exposure, such as sensitivity to the price of oil. The first of these is the direct consequence of being able to short: a long-only manager can act on a negative view only by holding none of the security, so the expression of that view is capped at the security's benchmark weight. Shorting removes that cap.
rationales.B: Only the market-neutral variants target zero exposure to the Market factor. A 130/30 long extension, for instance, retains 100% net exposure and is fully exposed to market risk, and a directional low-risk structure that is long 80 and short 40 retains 40% net exposure. The benefits actually claimed for long/short strategies are fuller expression of short ideas, efficient use of leverage and of diversification, and greater ability to calibrate exposure to factors, sectors, geography, and other undesired exposures.
rationales.C: Short-selling raises collateral demands rather than lowering them. To borrow securities the investor relies on a prime broker, who requires collateral to assure the securities lenders that their contracts will be honored, and the required amount grows with the relative amount of short-selling in the portfolio. Reduced collateral is therefore not among the benefits of a long/short strategy; it is one of its costs.

questions.stem: For a strategy that shorts securities, it is most likely that a short position:

options.A: never requires additional collateral once borrowed.
options.B: moves against the manager if the price rises.
options.C: can lose at most the amount initially invested.

rationales.A: Collateral requirements increase if a short position moves against the manager. In extreme cases the manager may be forced to liquidate some favorably ranked long positions, and short positions that might eventually have reversed, if too much leverage has been used. The borrow is therefore not the end of the collateral obligation but the start of it, and the obligation is marked continuously against the price of the shorted security.
rationales.B: Strategies that short securities carry four inherent risks. First, unlike a long position, a short position moves against the manager if the price of the security increases. Second, long/short strategies sometimes require significant leverage, which must be used wisely. Third, the cost of borrowing a security can become prohibitive, particularly if the security is hard to borrow. Fourth, collateral requirements increase if a short position moves against the manager; in extreme cases the manager may be forced to liquidate favorably ranked long positions, and short positions that might eventually reverse, if too much leverage has been used. The manager may also fall victim to a short squeeze, a situation in which the price of the shorted stock has risen so much and so quickly that many short investors are unable to maintain their positions in the short run given the increased collateral requirements. The squeeze worsens as short-sellers liquidate, buying back the security and possibly pushing the price higher still.
rationales.C: The loss on a short position is potentially unlimited, because the price of the shorted security can rise without bound, whereas the loss on a long position is capped at the amount invested. This asymmetry is what makes the other inherent risks bite: rising prices raise collateral requirements at the same time as they generate the loss, and in a short squeeze the two effects compound.

questions.stem: A prime broker's collateral requirement for a short position is most likely to:

options.A: count all asset types at full market value.
options.B: be fixed regardless of the portfolio's short intensity.
options.C: assure lenders that contracts will be honored.

rationales.A: Different types of assets are weighed differently in the calculation of collateral value. A US Treasury bill may be viewed as very safe and accorded 100% of its value toward the required collateral, while a high-yield bond or another asset with restricted liquidity has only a portion of its market value counted. Posting a given market value of collateral therefore does not satisfy a given requirement; what satisfies it depends on what the collateral is.
rationales.B: The higher the relative amount of short-selling in a portfolio, the greater the amount of collateral required. A portfolio with 20% of capital invested short may be required to put up collateral equal to 40% of the short positions, whereas a portfolio with 100% of capital invested short could be required to put up collateral equal to 200% of the short positions. The requirement scales with short intensity rather than staying fixed, and it also rises as existing short positions move against the manager.
rationales.C: To short-sell, investors typically rely on a prime broker who can help locate the securities they wish to borrow, and the prime broker requires collateral from the short-sellers to assure the lenders of those securities that their contracts will be honored. The amount scales with short intensity: a portfolio with 20% of capital invested short may post collateral equal to 40% of the short positions, while a portfolio with 100% of capital invested short could be required to post 200%. Asset types are also weighed differently in the calculation of collateral value - a US Treasury bill may count at 100% of its value, whereas a high-yield bond or another restricted-liquidity asset has only a portion of its market value counted.

questions.stem: Equal-risk-premium products are most likely to:

options.A: have no specified construction method.
options.B: be unable to isolate premiums across asset classes.
options.C: weight long/short sub-portfolios for equal risk contribution.

rationales.A: The construction is specified in detail: the manager builds a long/short sub-portfolio to extract each rewarded factor premium, then combines the sub-portfolios using weightings that ensure each contributes the same amount of risk to the overall portfolio, and the combination may be levered across all sub-portfolios to reach a target volatility. In the equitized version, market exposure is restored by running the market-neutral portfolio as an overlay, so neither the factor extraction nor the restoration of market exposure is left unexplained.
rationales.B: Equal-risk-premium products do exactly this. They seek to extract return premiums from rewarded factors, often across asset classes, by means of long/short sub-portfolios built factor by factor; the cross-asset reach is a feature of the design rather than an obstacle to it.
rationales.C: Equal-risk-premium products seek to extract return premiums from rewarded factors, often across asset classes. The manager creates long/short sub-portfolios that extract these premiums - Size, Value, Momentum, Low Beta - and combines them using weightings that ensure each component contributes the same amount of risk to the overall portfolio. The combination may then be levered across all sub-portfolios to achieve a specific volatility level: because removing the effect of the Market factor strips out the largest single source of volatility, such products often need three units of leverage long and short to reach a 10% absolute risk target. In the equitized version the investor is not abandoning equity-like returns at all, but is holding the market-neutral portfolio as an overlay on top of market exposure.
